Triggers.value: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, 'Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents' is a hard-to-explain trigger because it implies a transport/accident trauma context rather than disaster-related cues. This is not just unusual; it mismatches the stated trauma type and is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The Threat node includes 'Flashbacks', which is more a re-experiencing/memory phenomenon than a current threat belief or arousal cue. Given that Memory is structurally isolated in the formulation, placing a prominent memory-like item in Threat creates a formulation mismatch, especially when no Memory items are endorsed to support that link.

The trigger pattern is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of natural disaster. 'Being seen' and 'feeling watched or observed' imply an interpersonal/social-threat cue set rather than reminders of an impersonal disaster. With no memory items or appraisals referencing social judgment, persecution, or assault, these two trigger items look clinically mismatched to the trauma context.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals 'I am inadequate' and 'I can't rely on myself' can occur after trauma, but in this profile they pair mainly with social-observation triggers and do not connect clearly to a natural-disaster formulation. The remaining items emphasize generalized threat/hypervigilance, whereas these appraisals suggest a more interpersonal/shame-based presentation. That makes the profile as a whole less coherent.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, 'feeling watched or observed' is difficult to reconcile as a trauma-linked trigger. It suggests interpersonal persecution/surveillance rather than an environmental disaster cue, while the other trigger items are disaster-congruent.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: 'Scanning exits' is not impossible, but paired with a natural-disaster trauma and the other selected items it points toward man-made/interpersonal danger in enclosed spaces rather than the presented disaster context. This makes the threat profile feel partially mismatched to the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate
issues.explanation: The negative-appraisal set is otherwise about global damage and reduced self-reliance after trauma. 'I am inadequate' can occur in PTSD, but here it reads as a generalized self-worth theme without a clear link to the disaster-based trigger/threat pattern, making the appraisal node somewhat less coherent than the other two items.

vignette: Akua had always been drawn to the precision and control of surgery, but nothing could have prepared her for the day a devastating hurricane tore through her hometown in West Africa. She was 18 at the time, home from college for summer break, and had volunteered at a local hospital to gain experience. As the storm raged on, the hospital's generators failed, plunging the operating room into darkness. Akua watched in horror as a patient on the table began to flatline, and she felt powerless to save them. The memory of that moment still haunted her three years later, now a 21-year-old surgeon-in-training. Whenever a storm rolled in, with its familiar sounds of howling wind and creaking trees, Akua's heart would racing and her hands would begin to shake. She couldn't bear the thought of being trapped in a dark place again, so she avoided exercising outdoors or going for walks at night. Even waking up in the dark was enough to send her scrambling for the light switch. Akua had tried to convince herself that she was fine, that she just needed to "toughen up" and get on with her life. But as she delved deeper into her residency program, she found it increasingly difficult to control her emotions. She would lash out at colleagues over minor mistakes or become irrationally upset when a patient's vitals began to drop. Her usual composure in the operating room had given way to a constant sense of hypervigilance – every beeping monitor or rustling gown made her jump. When feeling threatened, Akua's instinct was to become overly compliant, desperate to avoid conflict or rejection. She would agree to take on extra shifts or cover for colleagues without hesitation, even if it meant sacrificing her own needs and well-being. This people-pleasing had earned her a reputation as a team player, but deep down, Akua felt like she was losing herself in the process. At times, Akua wondered if she was truly cut out to be a surgeon. The memory of that patient's flatline still echoed in her mind, and she couldn't shake the feeling that she was somehow responsible for their death. "My life has been destroyed by this trauma," she would whisper to herself in the dead of night, as the darkness seemed to closing in around her. Akua felt like she was living on edge, constantly waiting for the other shoe to drop. She had begun to doubt her own abilities and judgment, wondering if she could ever truly rely on herself again. The smallest setback or unexpected noise would send her into a spiral of anxiety, as she frantically tried to regain control. Despite her best efforts, Akua couldn't escape the sense that bad things were always lurking just out of sight, waiting to pounce. She had started to withdraw from social engagements and hobbies, preferring the safety of her own company to the uncertainty of the outside world. It was as if she was constantly holding her breath, bracing for impact. The final straw came when Akua found herself frozen in terror during a routine procedure, unable to move or speak as a sudden noise sent her careening back into that dark operating room. She knew then that she needed help – not just to cope with the symptoms, but to reclaim her sense of self and purpose. As she sat in the therapist's office, Akua felt a glimmer of hope that maybe, just maybe, she could learn to heal and find her way back to the confident, capable surgeon she once was.
